primer.isl_p_world.title: The House of Islam
primer.isl_p_world.text: You were born in Dar al-Islam, the "House of Islam", a world stretching from Spain to Central Asia. The head of all Muslims is the caliph, the "successor" of the Prophet Muhammad, though real power often lies with emirs and sultans. The language of faith, law and learning is Arabic; the money is the gold dinar and the silver dirham. A merchant can travel from Cordoba to Samarkand hearing the same call to prayer everywhere and finding a mosque, a bathhouse and a caravanserai in every town.
primer.isl_p_world_abbasid.title: The Abbasid caliphate
primer.isl_p_world_abbasid.text: In 750 the Abbasids, descendants of the Prophet's uncle, overthrew the Umayyads, and the caliphate's capital moved from Damascus to the east. In 762 Caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad on the Tigris - the Round City. Under Harun al-Rashid (786–809) and al-Ma'mun (813–833) Baghdad became one of the richest cities on earth, and in the House of Wisdom Greek and Indian books were translated. But over time a Turkish guard closes around the caliphs, and from 836 to 892 they even live in a new capital, Samarra.
primer.isl_p_world_buyid.title: A caliph without power
primer.isl_p_world_buyid.text: The caliph in Baghdad no longer rules in person. In 945 the city was taken by the Buyids, Shiites from mountainous Daylam, and in 1055 they were replaced by the Seljuk chief Tughril Beg, who took the title of sultan. The Islamic world has split: since 969 Cairo has had its own Fatimid caliphs, Ismailis, and in Cordoba an Umayyad declared himself caliph back in 929. Damascus changes hands from the Fatimids to the Seljuks. Meanwhile, under the Seljuk vizier Nizam al-Mulk, Nizamiyya colleges open in city after city.
primer.isl_p_world_crusades.title: The Franks and Saladin
primer.isl_p_world_crusades.text: Frankish crusaders have come from the West: in 1099 they took Jerusalem and founded their own states along the Syrian coast. Against them rose Zengi, his son Nur al-Din of Damascus and finally Salah al-Din - Saladin, a Kurd who abolished the Fatimid caliphate in Cairo in 1171 and in 1187 crushed the crusaders at Hattin and retook Jerusalem. His descendants, the Ayyubids, rule Egypt and Syria, while the Baghdad caliph al-Nasir has won back some of his old power.
primer.isl_p_world_baghdad_fall.title: The end of the caliphate
primer.isl_p_world_baghdad_fall.text: The caliphate in Baghdad is living out its last years. In February 1258 the Mongol khan Hulagu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, took the city; the story goes that the last caliph, al-Musta'sim, was rolled in a carpet and trampled by horses so that no royal blood would be spilled. Tens of thousands of townspeople died, and books from the libraries, it is said, were thrown into the Tigris until the water ran black with ink. Now Baghdad is a provincial town of the Ilkhanate, though its markets and canals slowly revive.
primer.isl_p_world_mamluk.title: The Mamluk sultans
primer.isl_p_world_mamluk.text: Egypt and Syria are ruled by the Mamluks - former slave soldiers, Turks and Circassians, bought as boys and raised in barracks. In 1260 at Ain Jalut their sultans Qutuz and Baybars stopped the Mongols, and in 1291 they drove the crusaders from their last fortress, Acre. A caliph of the Abbasid line lives in Cairo, but the sultan rules and the caliph merely blesses him. Disasters come too: the Black Death of 1348, and Timur, who sacked Damascus in 1401.
primer.isl_p_world_ottoman.title: The Ottomans arrive
primer.isl_p_world_ottoman.text: The Ottomans rule here now. In 1516 Sultan Selim I routed the Mamluks at Marj Dabiq near Aleppo, and in 1517 he took Cairo; the last Mamluk sultan, Tumanbay, was hanged at the Bab Zuwayla gate, and the last Cairo caliph was taken off to Istanbul. Suleiman the Magnificent (1520–1566) rules lands from Hungary to Yemen and Baghdad. Damascus and Cairo have become provinces governed by pashas sent from the capital.
primer.isl_p_world_istanbul.title: The sultans' capital
primer.isl_p_world_istanbul.text: In 1453 Mehmed II the Conqueror took Constantinople and made it his capital. The city, emptied under the last emperors, is being resettled: the sultans move Turks, Greeks and Armenians here, and in 1492 Bayezid II took in the Jews expelled from Spain. From here rule Selim I, conqueror of Egypt, and Suleiman the Magnificent, whose empire stretches from Buda to Baghdad. In the Topkapi Palace the Divan - the council of viziers - meets, and the sultan listens from behind a grille.
primer.isl_p_world_fatimid.title: The Fatimid caliphs
primer.isl_p_world_fatimid.text: Your city is young: in 969 the general Jawhar, on the orders of Caliph al-Mu'izz, founded al-Qahira, "the Victorious", beside old Fustat. The Fatimids are Ismaili Shiites who trace their line to Fatima, the Prophet's daughter, though most Egyptians are Sunnis or Copts. The strange caliph al-Hakim (996–1021) banned eating mulukhiyya and forbade women to go out in the street, and under al-Mustansir in the 1060s years of famine and strife ravaged the city. More and more, power lies with soldier-viziers.
primer.isl_p_world_cordoba_emirate.title: The Umayyad emirate
primer.isl_p_world_cordoba_emirate.text: In 756 Abd al-Rahman I arrived here - the only Umayyad to escape the massacre carried out by the Abbasids - and became emir of al-Andalus. The caliph in Baghdad is not obeyed here. Abd al-Rahman began building the Great Mosque with its forest of columns and two-coloured arches, and his descendants keep enlarging it. Christians are still the majority, but their children increasingly speak Arabic and embrace Islam; in the 850s some Cordoban Christians even sought martyrdom by publicly denouncing the Prophet.
primer.isl_p_world_cordoba_caliphate.tex: In 929 Emir Abd al-Rahman III proclaimed himself caliph - now Muslims have three caliphs: in Baghdad, the Fatimids in Africa, and here. Cordoba is one of the largest cities in Europe, and the library of Caliph al-Hakam II, tradition says, holds 400,000 volumes. Outside the city rose the palace-city of Madinat al-Zahra. From 978 the real ruler is the chamberlain al-Mansur - Christians call him Almanzor; in 997 he sacked Santiago de Compostela. After his death in 1002, strife will tear the caliphate apart.
primer.isl_p_world_cordoba_taifa.title: Taifas and Reconquista
primer.isl_p_world_cordoba_taifa.text: The caliphate of Cordoba has fallen apart: it was abolished in 1031, and al-Andalus split into taifas - small emirates that fight each other and pay tribute to Christian kings. Cordoba is no longer a capital, though the philosopher Ibn Rushd (1126) and the physician and sage Maimonides (1138) were born here. Stern Berber Almoravids came from Africa to help (1091), then the Almohads, but the Christians keep advancing: in 1236 Ferdinand III of Castile will take the city.
primer.isl_p_society.title: Who is on top
primer.isl_p_society.text: Before God all Muslims are equal, but in practice society is a ladder. At the top are the caliph or sultan, his emirs and viziers, and soldiers granted an iqta - the right to collect a land's taxes instead of pay. Below them are the ulama, scholars of faith and law, rich merchants, master craftsmen of the bazaar and fellahin, the peasants. Christians and Jews are dhimmi, "protected people" who pay a poll tax, the jizya. At the bottom are slaves - though here a slave soldier can even become sultan.
primer.isl_p_society_slave.title: In bondage
primer.isl_p_society_slave.text: You were born in bondage. Slaves are brought from afar: Turks from the steppes, Slavs - the saqaliba - from Europe, Africans from across the Sahara and the upper Nile. Islam does not forbid slavery, but it commands kindness to slaves and counts freeing one as a good deed. If a master acknowledges a child by a slave woman, the child is free, and the mother too goes free when her master dies - she is called umm walad, "mother of a child". A slave in a great house can become its steward, and a slave soldier an emir.
primer.isl_p_society_peasant.title: The fellahin
primer.isl_p_society_peasant.text: Your family are fellahin, peasants. You plough with a wooden ard and grow wheat, barley and dates, and in Egypt and Iraq life depends on water: the Nile flood or the canals of the Tigris and Euphrates, which the whole village must clear every year. From the harvest you pay the kharaj, the land tax - sometimes as much as half the crop - and the village's revenue often goes not to the treasury but to an emir holding it as his iqta. With the spread of Islam came sugar cane, rice, cotton and oranges.
primer.isl_p_society_noble.title: A noble house
primer.isl_p_society_noble.text: Your family is among the great. You have a house with an inner courtyard and fountain, servants and slaves, and the men serve at court: the vizier runs the treasury and decrees, the emir commands troops, the qadi judges. Nobles live on the income of iqtas and estates, but a ruler's favour is fickle: the Barmakids, all-powerful viziers of Harun al-Rashid, lost everything in a single night in 803, and their head, Ja'far, was executed. Sons learn the Quran, calligraphy, archery, riding and eloquence.
primer.isl_p_birth.title: First words of God
primer.isl_p_birth.text: Among Muslims, as soon as a child is born, the father or an elder whispers the adhan, the call to prayer, into its right ear, so that the first words it hears are the name of God. The baby's palate is touched with a chewed date. On the seventh day it is named - Muhammad, Ahmad, Ali, Fatima, Aisha - its hair is shaved, its weight in silver is given to the poor, and if the family can afford it a ram is slaughtered: the aqiqa. Christians and Jews have their own rites - baptism, and circumcision on the eighth day.
primer.isl_p_childhood.title: School and games
primer.isl_p_childhood.text: Children are breastfed until two - as the Quran advises - often by a wet nurse. Little ones play in courtyards and on flat roofs with knucklebones, tops, balls and clay horses; jurists allow girls dolls, since tradition says Aisha, the Prophet's wife, played with dolls as a child. From about six, boys go to the kuttab, a primary school by the mosque, where they chant suras of the Quran in chorus and trace letters on a wooden board. Craftsmen's children go early to the bazaar as apprentices.
primer.isl_p_home.title: A house facing inward
primer.isl_p_home.text: Houses here face inward: the street sees only blank walls and a stout door, and life goes on in the inner courtyard with its well, tree or fountain. Windows are screened with carved wooden lattices, mashrabiyya, which let in the cool breeze but not a stranger's gaze. People sit and sleep on carpets, cushions and low divans, eat from a shared tray, and in the heat sleep out on the flat roof. The women's part of the house, the harim, is closed to men from outside the family.
primer.isl_p_food.title: Dates and sherbet
primer.isl_p_food.text: The staples are bread, dates, lentils, olive oil and yoghurt; the poor eat mutton on feast days. Islam forbids pork and wine, though Baghdad poets like Abu Nuwas sang of wine in verse. In tenth-century Baghdad al-Warraq compiled a cookbook with hundreds of recipes: harisa of wheat and meat, sweet halwa, sherbets chilled with snow brought down from the mountains. During the month of Ramadan Muslims eat only between sunset and dawn.
primer.isl_p_clothes.title: Turbans and muslin
primer.isl_p_clothes.text: Men wear a long shirt, a caftan and a cloak, with a turban on the head whose size shows rank: the ulama wear enormous ones. Women go out covered by a veil from head to toe, and at home wear trousers, embroidered dresses and bracelets. The cloth of these lands is famous worldwide - muslin is named after Mosul, damask after Damascus, and tiraz, bands woven with the caliph's name, are given as a mark of favour. The law sometimes requires non-Muslims to wear special belts or colours.
primer.isl_p_faith.title: The five pillars
primer.isl_p_faith.text: Most people follow Islam. Five times a day the muezzin calls to prayer from the minaret; on Fridays men gather in the great mosque for the khutba sermon; and in Ramadan the whole city fasts until sunset. Every Muslim gives zakat - a share of their wealth to the poor - and hopes to make the hajj to Mecca at least once. The ulama, scholars of the Quran and law, are more respected than the rich, and Sufi mystics meet in their lodges to seek closeness to God through dhikr, the repetition of His names.
primer.isl_p_faith_christian.title: Christians as dhimmi
primer.isl_p_faith_christian.text: You are a Christian - there are many here, and under Muslim law you are dhimmi, "protected people". You pay the jizya, may not build new churches without permission or ring bells loudly, but you live by your own laws and your bishops settle your disputes. Christians here are of many kinds: Nestorians of Iraq, Jacobites of Syria, Melkites, Copts of Egypt, and under the Ottomans Greeks and Armenians. Many serve rulers as scribes and physicians: the Nestorian Bukhtishu family were doctors to the Abbasids for generations.
primer.isl_p_faith_mozarab.title: The Mozarabs
primer.isl_p_faith_mozarab.text: You are a Mozarab, one of the Christians of al-Andalus living under Muslim rule. You worship by the old Visigothic rite but speak Arabic, bear Arabic names and love Arabic poetry - back in the ninth century the Cordoban writer Alvarus complained that young men could not write a letter in Latin yet composed Arabic odes. As dhimmi you pay the jizya and are judged by your own count and judges. Over the years the communities shrink: some embrace Islam, others move to the Christian north.
primer.isl_p_faith_jewish.title: The Jewish community
primer.isl_p_faith_jewish.text: You come from the Jewish community - Jews live in every large city, with their own synagogues, courts and community head. As dhimmi you pay the jizya but may trade, practise medicine and serve: in tenth-century Cordoba the physician Hasdai ibn Shaprut advised the caliph, and in Cairo lived Maimonides, physician at the Ayyubid court and a great scholar. The letters of Cairo's Jews piled up for centuries in the geniza, a storeroom of the Ben Ezra synagogue, and tell of trade from Spain to India.
primer.isl_p_faith_zoroastrian.title: Keepers of the fire
primer.isl_p_faith_zoroastrian.text: You are a Zoroastrian, a follower of the ancient faith of the Persian kings. You pray before a sacred fire that burns in the temple without ever going out, and you guard the purity of water and earth, so the dead are not buried but laid in towers of silence. Muslim law counts you as dhimmi, like Christians and Jews, and you pay the jizya. But the communities are dwindling: generation after generation more of your people embrace Islam, and some, tradition says, sailed away to India, where they are called Parsis.
primer.isl_p_work.title: Bazaar and caravans
primer.isl_p_work.text: The Islamic world is one vast market from the Atlantic to India. Every city has its souk, where each trade has its own street - coppersmiths, weavers, perfumers, booksellers - and the muhtasib checks weights and prices. Merchants lead camel caravans and sail to India and China, paying not only in gold dinars and silver dirhams but with notes called sakk that can be cashed in another city. The European word "cheque" is thought to come from it.
primer.isl_p_place.title: Deserts and oases
primer.isl_p_place.text: The Islamic world is deserts and oases, great rivers and noisy cities. It is hot and dry, so everything depends on water: canals, wells, underground channels called qanats, and creaking water wheels, norias. Every city has its great mosque, bazaar, hammam baths and caravanserais where merchants stay the night with their camels. Caravan routes run from city to city, and dhows with slanting triangular sails ply the seas.
primer.isl_p_place_baghdad.title: The City of Peace
primer.isl_p_place_baghdad.text: Baghdad is called Madinat al-Salam, "the City of Peace". Caliph al-Mansur built it round: double walls about two kilometres across, four gates, and at the centre a palace with a green dome and the great mosque. The city soon outgrew its walls and spread along both banks of the Tigris, where thousands of boats dart about. In the markets of Karkh they sell paper, silk, Chinese porcelain and books, and the population, by various estimates, runs to several hundred thousand - more than any city in Europe.
primer.isl_p_place_damascus.title: The Ghouta oasis
primer.isl_p_place_damascus.text: Damascus lies in the green oasis of the Ghouta below Mount Qasiyun, its gardens watered by the Barada river split into dozens of channels. At its heart stands the Umayyad Mosque, built by Caliph al-Walid around 715 on the site of the cathedral of John the Baptist; the saint's head is believed to rest inside. The city is famous for its sword steel, brocade, rosewater and apricots, and every year a great caravan of pilgrims sets out from its gates for Mecca.
primer.isl_p_place_cairo.title: City on the Nile
primer.isl_p_place_cairo.text: Cairo lives by the Nile. Every year in late summer the river floods, and on the day the water reaches the right mark on the Nilometer on Roda Island, the city celebrates: there will be a harvest. Above the roofs rise hundreds of minarets and the al-Azhar mosque, where students come from all over the Islamic world, and from the late twelfth century the Citadel on its hill, begun by Saladin. The streets are packed with donkeys, camels and hawkers, and in Ibn Battuta's words the crowds surge here like the waves of the sea.
primer.isl_p_place_cordoba.title: Ornament of the world
primer.isl_p_place_cordoba.text: Cordoba stands on the Guadalquivir, spanned by an old Roman bridge. Its heart is the Great Mosque, a forest of hundreds of columns and red-and-white striped arches, with orange trees growing in its courtyard. The streets are paved, water murmurs in the courtyards, dozens of bathhouses are open, and in the evenings the strings of the oud are heard. The nun Hrotsvitha in faraway Saxony, who heard of the city from envoys, called Cordoba "the ornament of the world".
primer.isl_p_place_istanbul.title: City between two seas
primer.isl_p_place_istanbul.text: Istanbul, once Constantinople, is again one of the largest cities in the world: by the late sixteenth century it has, by various estimates, 400,000 people or more. Mosques with slender minarets crown its hills - among them the Süleymaniye of the architect Sinan (1557) - the Topkapi Palace stands on the point, and the Covered Bazaar holds thousands of shops. Caiques dart across the Golden Horn, European merchants live in Galata, and from the mid-sixteenth century coffeehouses appear where people argue over the news.
primer.isl_p_law.title: Sharia and the qadi
primer.isl_p_law.text: The law here is the sharia, "the way", which scholars derive from the Quran and the Prophet's sunna. Sunnis have four schools of law - Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali - and every city has its qadi, a judge who hears cases in the mosque or at home. Witnesses count for more than documents, and an oath before God is a serious matter. The law prescribes cutting off a thief's hand, but the conditions are so many that beatings, fines or prison are far more common.
primer.isl_p_health.title: Hospitals
primer.isl_p_health.text: Medicine here is among the best in the world: doctors study Galen and Hippocrates in Arabic translation, and works of their own - al-Razi, who first described the difference between smallpox and measles, and Ibn Sina, author of the Canon of Medicine. Large cities have bimaristans, hospitals where treatment is free; in Sultan Qalawun's hospital in Cairo (1284), it is said, musicians even played for the sick. Yet fevers, dysentery and plague still kill: the Black Death of 1348 carried off perhaps a third of the townspeople.
primer.isl_p_women.title: Dower and harem
primer.isl_p_women.text: A girl is married off by her parents, and her consent is sought in different ways: a virgin's silence is often taken as a yes. The groom pays the mahr, a marriage gift that remains the wife's own property. A man may take up to four wives if he supports them equally, but only a few rich men do. A woman owns her property and inheritance outright and can bring a case before the qadi; divorce is easy for a husband, harder but possible for a wife. Noblewomen build mosques and fountains with their own money.
primer.isl_p_leisure.title: Eid and Ramadan nights
primer.isl_p_leisure.text: The great feasts are Eid al-Fitr, breaking the Ramadan fast, and Eid al-Adha, the feast of sacrifice, when a ram is slaughtered and its meat shared with the poor. Ramadan nights are lively: after sunset the streets fill with people, sweets and lights. Adults play chess and backgammon, listen to storytellers in the squares and musicians with the oud; nobles hunt with falcons and play polo. People spend half a day in the hammam - for cleanliness, rest and all the town gossip.
primer.isl_p_knowledge.title: Paper and algebra
primer.isl_p_knowledge.text: People here love books. Legend says that after the battle of Talas in 751 Chinese captives taught the craftsmen of Samarkand to make paper, and soon paper mills were working in Baghdad and hundreds of shops opened in the booksellers' market. In the House of Wisdom Aristotle, Euclid and Ptolemy were translated; al-Khwarizmi wrote a book on al-jabr - hence "algebra" - and numerals arrived from India. Boys learn in the kuttab by the mosque, young men in the madrasa, where scholars spend years expounding the Quran and law.
primer.isl_p_war.title: Ghulams and ghazis
primer.isl_p_war.text: Wars are almost constant: with the Romans on the Anatolian frontier, with the Frankish crusaders, the Mongols, the Christian kings of Spain - and Muslim rulers often fight each other too. The armies of caliphs and sultans are increasingly made up of ghulams and mamluks - Turks bought as boys and trained to shoot from the saddle. On the frontiers volunteer ghazis go raiding, believing that whoever falls for the faith goes to paradise. A soldier serves not for pay but for an iqta - the revenue of a few villages.
primer.isl_p_war_ottoman.title: Janissaries and cannon
primer.isl_p_war_ottoman.text: The great military power of the age is the Ottoman army. At its core are the Janissaries, the "new troops": boys from Christian villages in the Balkans are taken in the devshirme, the levy of children, converted to Islam and raised as the sultan's soldiers. They may not marry, live in barracks, draw a salary and increasingly fight with muskets. The sultans' cannon breached the walls of Constantinople in 1453, and under Suleiman the Ottomans besieged Vienna (1529) and fight the Safavids of Iran and the Spanish fleet.
